source.title: The Effect of Batch Size on Contrastive Self-Supervised Speech Representation Learning

page_placements.theme: Batch-size effects depend on workload, recipe and budget

record.file_problem: None; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests batch-size effects on downstream speech-recognition error in a new modality and training setup. The paper does not test the claim's fixed-epoch image-classification or language-model conditions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports speech-recognition WER after wav2vec 2.0 pretraining at multiple batch sizes, plus gradient variability and codebook statistics. Rows below capture the primary batch-size comparison for 10 minutes of fine-tuning labels. Table III reports more label amounts, decoding methods, and test sets; Table IV reports overlapping-data comparisons; those additional results are not fully extracted.
record.test_reason: The study measures downstream speech-recognition WER after contrastive speech pretraining, rather than held-out performance of image classifiers or language models as specified by V5. Its main sweep also changes training exposure with batch size; separate matched-exposure comparisons address a related speech-learning claim. None of V1–V8 is directly tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate: total speech exposure is the main predictor of downstream performance, allowing smaller batches to compensate through more iterations. The authors identify approximately 150 seconds as the convergence minimum and 40 minutes as the point of diminishing returns in this setup. They also report some degradation at 80 minutes and suggest stronger regularization as a possible remedy, without testing that remedy.
record.recipe_differences: Independent wav2vec 2.0 BASE implementation; self-supervised speech pretraining and downstream ASR rather than the claim's natural-label image or language classification settings. Fixed iteration comparisons change the amount of data seen; separate comparisons match data seen across batch sizes.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch duration, number of pretraining iterations and total observed speech, amount of labeled fine-tuning data, and test set. The authors also state that 80-minute performance can be worse than 40-minute performance on test-other with at least 10 hours of labels.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger speech-pretraining batches generally improve downstream WER when training iterations are approximately fixed, while also increasing total speech exposure. The selected 80-minute checkpoint uses fewer iterations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For wav2vec 2.0 speech pretraining, increasing batch duration generally improves downstream ASR performance under an iteration budget, with diminishing returns.

fits_no_version.finding: Matched-exposure checkpoints generally have similar downstream WER. At 66.7k hours seen, batches of 10, 20, 40, and 80 minutes yield test-clean WERs of 9.07, 9.28, 8.63, and 9.29 after fine-tuning with 100 hours of labels.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within converging wav2vec 2.0 speech-pretraining settings, total speech exposure largely predicts downstream ASR performance across batch sizes and iteration counts.

record.problems: One model family and one speech dataset; learning rates were selected by heuristics and the authors acknowledge a more independent search might improve results. No uncertainty estimates are reported. The batch-size sweep uses fixed iterations, so batch size also changes the total data observed.
record.rows_left_out: Table III contains additional fine-tuning label amounts, test sets, and decoding methods; Table IV gives the overlapping-data comparisons across multiple batch sizes and checkpoints. They are not exhaustively extracted here. Figure 4's gradient-variance measurement is omitted because it measures gradient variability, not held-out performance or the training-test gap.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, natural-label generalization, and chance performance on random held-out labels.
Width scaling beyond zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer performance under different tuning budgets.
Large-batch penalties and their recovery in image classifiers or language models under fixed epoch budgets.
Controlled dropout effects on held-out error.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, training–test gaps, and comparison with other generalization measures.
Removing memorized examples versus removing random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Table III and Table IV omissions are already declared in rows_left_out. The extracted numerical values are correct, but the first proposed verdict mistakes improving WER with larger batches for support of a large-batch penalty. The second proposed verdict contradicts its own numerical comparison. The prose's stated test-other exception is broader than Table III supports.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Fixed-epoch comparisons; image classifiers and language models; recipe adaptations such as warmup or normalization changes.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to the generalization gap.

relation.reason: Section II-A discusses batch size, generalization, training budgets and regularization; its own experiments do not test a listed claim version.

tranche.reason: Measures downstream ASR after contrastive speech pretraining, outside V5's image-classifier and language-model settings. The matched-exposure comparison addresses a related transfer-performance question.

source_check.notes: Table IV, p. 14, confirms all four cited WER percentages. Section IV-C2 specifies letter decoding; 66.7k hours is nominal cumulative exposure (an upper bound), with 400k, 200k, 100k and 50k pretraining iterations respectively.
